title: Java Booleans
learningObjectives: Declare boolean variables using true or false.
Build boolean expressions with comparison operators.
Combine conditions using logical AND, OR and NOT.
Use boolean expressions to control an if/else decision.
Explain short-circuit evaluation and avoid confusing boolean values with text.

understand.concept: The boolean type represents one of two values: true or false. Boolean expressions are produced by comparisons and logical operations, and they are commonly used to control decisions and loops.
understand.whyItMatters: Programs need to make decisions: whether a user is eligible, a stock item is available, a payment is approved or a score meets a threshold. Boolean expressions represent these conditions directly.
understand.analogy: A boolean is like a yes/no decision on a checklist: the answer is either true or false.
understand.analogyLimit: Real-world decisions may involve uncertainty, missing information or more than two states. A boolean alone cannot explain why a decision was made or represent an unknown state.

explain.narrative:
## Boolean values

A boolean variable can contain only `true` or `false`:

```java
boolean isAvailable = true;
boolean paymentComplete = false;
```

These are boolean literals, not text. The Strings `"true"` and `"false"` are different values with a different type.

## Expressions that produce booleans

Comparison operators such as `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `==` and `!=` produce boolean results. For example, `stock > 0` is true when stock is positive.

## Combining conditions

- `&&` requires both conditions to be true.
- `||` requires at least one condition to be true.
- `!` reverses a boolean expression.

The conditional AND and OR operators use short-circuit evaluation. For `a && b`, Java does not evaluate b when a is false. For `a || b`, Java does not evaluate b when a is true. This can help guard operations, but conditions should remain understandable.

## Using booleans in decisions

An if statement executes its first block when the condition is true; an else block can handle the false case:

```java
if (stock > 0) {
    System.out.println("Available");
} else {
    System.out.println("Out of stock");
}
```

## Common mistakes

- Assigning the String `"true"` to a boolean variable.
- Using `=` instead of a comparison operator.
- Writing a condition that is always true or always false by mistake.
- Using `&` or `|` when short-circuit `&&` or `||` is intended.
- Forgetting that boolean values do not explain the reason behind a decision.

practise.guidedTask: Create a boolean variable named isEligible using a score comparison. Use if/else to print an appropriate message for true and false cases.
practise.independentTask: Model an online order decision with boolean values for paymentComplete and addressVerified. Combine them with && and print whether the order can be processed.
hints: Use true and false without quotation marks.
Use && when every required condition must be true.
practise.challenge: Add a third condition for stock availability. Write a single readable expression that allows processing only when payment is complete, the address is verified and stock is available.

questions.prompt: Which values can a boolean variable store?
questions.explanation: Java's boolean type has exactly two values: true and false.
Logical AND is true only when both operands are true.
The logical NOT operator reverses a boolean value.

questions.prompt: When does the else block execute in an if/else statement?
options: When the if condition is false
When the if condition is true
questions.answer: When the if condition is false
questions.explanation: The else block provides the alternative path when the condition evaluates to false.

questions.prompt: Which is a boolean literal rather than a String?
questions.explanation: false without quotation marks is a boolean literal; quotation marks make text.
